title: The Goddess Who Stood Between
subtitle: Kottavi intervenes, and Krishna puts away his discus
story:
After the high-souled Krishna and Rudra had retired from the field, the hair-stirring battle of Sonitpura did not end — it changed hands. The war between Krishna and Vana, the thousand-armed king who was Shiva's devotee, had drawn the gods onto the battlefield, and now the younger commanders took it up.

Kartikeya, mounted on the car that Kumbhanda had brought him, drove straight at Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna and struck them with hundreds of dreadful, sharpened arrows. Bathed in blood, the three heroes fought back like three fires. When they struck Kartikeya with the three weapons given by the Wind-god, the Fire-god and Indra, he counteracted them with three weapons of his own — Shaila, Varuna and Savitri — and the Yadavas, by their illusory power, devoured even those, though the holder of the burning bow and shaft shot them swiftly.

Then Guha, burning with effulgence and biting his lips, took up the dreadful weapon called Brahmashira, like the Destroyer himself. When it was discharged — blazing with the effulgence of a thousand suns, destructive of the world — creatures lost consciousness at its warmth and fled on all sides, and the whole universe bewailed. Keshava, the slayer of Keshi, saw it and raised his discus, the destroyer and counteractor of all weapons; and as clouds in the rainy season cover the rays of the sun, so that discus covered the lustre of the Brahmashira and left it shorn of its power and energy.

Kartikeya's eyes reddened in anger, and he blazed up like fire to which clarified butter has been offered. He took up the golden Sakti — the celestial spear, set with bells, sure of aim, destructive of enemies, effulgent like a fire-brand and resembling the fire of dissolution — and hurled it with a shout that struck terror into his enemies. The spear flew into the sky, yawned, and moved about with great force, as if it desired to slay Krishna. The gods and their king were greatly depressed: "Perhaps Krishna will be consumed." But as the great spear appeared before him, Madhava shouted — as if remonstrating with it — and struck it down to the ground. "Well done! Well done!" rose from all sides, and Indra together with the celestials sent up a leonine shout.

Then Vasudeva, powerful, took up his discus to kill the Daityas. And he was about to discharge it when the beautiful Kottavi came before him — naked, at the command of Mahadeva, to protect Kumara. Lamva, the eighth portion of the goddess, intervened between them like a beautiful golden spear.

Seeing the goddess stand before Kartikeya, the large-armed Krishna was baffled. "Fie on you! Fly away soon from this place. Why do you throw obstacles in the way of certain destruction?"

Kottavi heard him — and for the sake of protecting Kumara, she did not put on her cloth.

"Take Guha with you," Krishna said, "and fly away soon from the battlefield. It will be well for us today if you do this. Or else, if I refrain from fighting, he will fight with me."

And beholding the naked goddess in the battlefield, the divine Hari put away his discus.

Then the goddess brought Guha before Hara, and the great danger passed. When Vana saw Kartikeya released from Krishna's discus and retiring from the field, he felt the inclination to fight Madhava himself. His ghosts, his Yakshas and his soldiers fled away on all sides; of that broken army only the Pramathas remained. And with them, and with his great Daitya commanders, Vana marched out to battle — while his priests and other elders, well read in the Shrutis, performed benedictory ceremonies on his behalf with mantras, recitations and herbs, chanting the destruction of his enemies.
reflection: Krishna's discus has never hesitated before a weapon, but it stops before a woman who stands unarmed. The episode turns on a strange kind of strength: the goddess does not fight, she merely refuses to move, and in that refusal the shape of the battle is changed.
content_note: The episode centers on the goddess Kottavi appearing unclothed on the battlefield; the source treats this matter-of-factly, and the story describes it with restraint.
next_story_tease: With Kartikeya withdrawn, Vana himself now took the field, roaring of his thousand arms.
hero_scene: Krishna, discus raised to strike, frozen mid-throw as the goddess Kottavi stands unclothed and unafraid before the young Kartikeya, her form gleaming between them like a golden spear.
visual_elements: the golden Sakti struck down on the ground
Vana marching out with his Daitya commanders
